title: Solid shapes: what rolls and what slides

summary.text: Put a ball and a matchbox on a sloping book. The ball runs away. The matchbox sits still. Why? And what about a round tin, which has flat ends and a curved side? You will test balls, boxes, tins and cones on a slope you build yourself. You will find out which part of a thing makes it roll, which part makes it slide, and which shapes you can stack into a tower.
summary.art: A girl kneeling beside a big book propped up on other books as a slope, letting go of a ball at the top while a matchbox sits still beside it.

intro.hook: You put these four on a slope. Which ones will roll away?
intro.text: The ball rolls away. So does the tin lying on its side. The cone rolls in a curve. The box does not roll at all: it stays, or it slides if the slope is steep. The ball, the tin and the cone each have a curved surface. The box has only flat faces. In this lesson you will test this on your own slope, and find one thing that can roll and slide.
intro.art: A ball, a matchbox, a round tin lying on its side and a paper cone lined up at the top of a sloping board.

outcomes: I can tell a solid shape from a flat shape.
I can find the flat faces and the curved surface of a thing by touching it.
I can say which things will roll and which will slide, and give the reason.
I can sort things into balls, boxes, tins and cones.
I can say which shapes stack, and why.
I can show that one thing, such as a tin, can roll one way up and slide another way up.

terms.meaning: A shape that is not flat. You can hold it in your hand, and it takes up room.
terms.example: A circle drawn on paper is flat. A ball is solid.
terms.art: A circle drawn on a sheet of paper next to a real ball resting on the same sheet.

terms.meaning: A flat part on the outside of a solid shape. Your whole palm can rest on it.
terms.example: A matchbox has 6 flat faces. Put your palm on the biggest one.
terms.art: A child's palm resting flat on the top face of a matchbox.

terms.meaning: A part on the outside of a solid shape that bends round. Your palm cannot lie flat on it.
terms.example: The side of a round tin is a curved surface. So is all of a ball.
terms.art: A child's hand wrapped round the curved side of a round tin.

terms.meaning: To move by turning over and over.
terms.example: A ball rolls down a slope. So does a pencil on a tilted desk.
terms.art: A ball on a slope with a curved arrow showing that it turns as it moves.

terms.meaning: To move along without turning over. The same face stays on the ground.
terms.example: A matchbox slides down a steep slope. You slide down a slide in the park.
terms.art: A matchbox on a steep slope with a straight arrow showing it moving down without turning.

terms.meaning: A surface with one end higher than the other.
terms.example: Put books under one end of a tray. The tray is now a slope.
terms.art: A steel tray with one end resting on a pile of three books.

terms.meaning: To put things one on top of another so that they stay.
terms.example: You can stack matchboxes. You cannot stack lemons.
terms.art: A neat tower of four matchboxes next to two lemons that have rolled apart.

terms.meaning: A solid shape that is curved all over. It has no flat face.
terms.example: A cricket ball, a marble and a laddu are ball shapes.
terms.art: A cricket ball, a glass marble and a laddu in a row.

terms.meaning: A solid shape with 6 flat faces and no curved surface.
terms.example: A matchbox, a dice, a brick and a book are box shapes.
terms.art: A matchbox, a dice, a brick and a closed book in a row.

terms.meaning: A solid shape with 2 flat round faces and 1 curved surface between them. A tin is also called a can.
terms.example: A round dabba, a new candle and a rolling pin are tin shapes.
terms.art: A round steel dabba, a candle and a rolling pin lying side by side.

terms.meaning: A solid shape with 1 flat round face, 1 curved surface and a point at the other end.
terms.example: An ice-cream cone, a party cap and a funnel are cones.
terms.art: An ice-cream cone, a paper party cap and a kitchen funnel in a row.

explanations.concept: A solid shape is a shape you can hold
explanations.context: In the Slope Test you held a ball, a box, a tin and a cone. This card says how they differ from shapes drawn on paper.
explanations.definition: A solid shape is not flat. It has a top, a bottom and sides, and it takes up room.
explanations.description: Draw round a coin on paper. You get a circle. It is flat, and you cannot pick it up. Now pick up a ball. You can close your hand round it, so it is solid. A flat shape lives on paper, or on one face of a thing. A solid shape is the whole thing. Now you try with a rectangle on paper and a matchbox.
examples: A circle on paper is flat. A ball is solid.
A rectangle on paper is flat. A matchbox is solid.
A picture of a laddu is flat. The laddu on your plate is solid.

perspectives.explanation: In his Elements, about 300 BCE, a solid is that which has length, breadth and depth. Greek thinkers such as Plato studied the five regular solids.
Mathematicians who study shapes by stretching and bending say a mug and a doughnut are the same solid shape, since each has one hole. For them the exact shape matters less than how it connects.

explanations.art: A circle and a rectangle drawn on a sheet of paper, with a real ball and a real matchbox sitting beside them.

explanations.context: In the Slope Test you felt each thing with your palm. This card names the two kinds of outside a solid shape can have.
explanations.definition: A flat face is a flat part of the outside. A curved surface is a part that bends round.
explanations.description: Hold a round tin. Put your palm on the lid. It lies flat, so the lid is a flat face. The bottom is a flat face too, which makes 2. Now wrap your hand round the side. Your palm has to bend, so the side is a curved surface. Now count the flat faces of a matchbox: top, bottom, front, back and two ends.
examples: A matchbox: 6 flat faces, no curved surface.
A round tin: 2 flat faces, 1 curved surface.
A cone: 1 flat face, 1 curved surface.
A ball: no flat face. It is curved all over.

perspectives.explanation: A flat face is a perfect plane and a curved surface is a perfect curve. These are ideas that real things only come near.
Look closer, and no table is perfectly flat. Its surface is made of tiny hills and valleys of atoms. 'Flat' depends on how closely we look.

explanations.art: A matchbox, a round tin, a paper cone and a ball in a row, each with its flat faces shaded in one colour.

explanations.concept: A curved surface rolls. A flat face slides.
explanations.context: In the Slope Test some things ran down a gentle slope and some waited for a steep one. This card gives the rule you found.
explanations.definition: A thing rolls when its curved surface is on the ground. A thing slides when a flat face is on the ground.
explanations.description: Put a ball on a gentle slope. Only a tiny spot of the ball touches the slope. The ball tips over on to the next spot, and the next. That is rolling. Now put a matchbox on the same slope. A whole flat face touches the slope and grips it, so the box stays. Make the slope steep. Now the box moves down with the same face on the slope all the way, and that is sliding.
examples: A marble rolls off a tilted plate at once.
A book stays on a tilted desk until the desk is steep.
A dice does not roll down a slope. It slides.

perspectives.explanation: A ball rolls, a box slides. It depends on which part touches the ground.
Rolling also needs friction between the ground and the object. On smooth ice a ball may slide without turning. A cube can tumble over its edges, as a die does.

explanations.art: Two slopes side by side: on the gentle one a ball is rolling, on the steep one a matchbox is sliding with the same face down.

explanations.context: In the Slope Test the round tin went into two heaps. This card says why one thing can be a roller and a slider.
explanations.definition: A thing with a curved surface and a flat face can roll or slide. It depends on which part is on the ground.
explanations.description: Lay a round tin on its side. Its curved surface is on the ground, so it rolls. Now stand the same tin on its end. A flat face is on the ground, so it stays, or slides if the slope is steep. Nothing about the tin changed. Only the part that touches the ground changed. A cone does the same: it stays on its flat face and rolls on its side. So always ask which part is touching the ground.
examples: A coin on its edge rolls. A coin lying flat slides.
A bangle on its edge rolls. A bangle lying down stays.
A glue stick lying down rolls off the desk. Standing up, it stays.
explanations.art: The same round tin drawn twice on a slope: lying on its side and rolling, and standing on its end and staying.
explanations.one_view: I asked about scale, scientists, traditions, other beings and history and found no second view. The idea that a tin can roll on its curved side or slide on its flat end is a plain test anyone can repeat with the same result.

explanations.concept: Four families: balls, boxes, tins and cones
explanations.context: This card sorts the things from the Slope Test into four families of solid shapes.
explanations.definition: Many things around us are close to one of four solid shapes: a ball, a box, a tin or a cone.
explanations.description: To find the family, feel the thing. Curved all over, with no flat face: a ball shape. Six flat faces and nothing curved: a box shape. Two flat round faces and a curved side: a tin shape. One flat round face, a curved side and a point: a cone. Size does not matter, so a marble and a football are both ball shapes. Many things, such as a spoon or a banana, fit no family. In later classes you will learn the maths names: sphere, cuboid, cylinder and cone.
examples: Ball shapes: a marble, a football, a laddu, a pea.
Box shapes: a matchbox, a dice, a brick, a soap box.
Tin shapes: a round dabba, a candle, a rolling pin, a drum.
Cones: an ice-cream cone, a party cap, a funnel.

perspectives.explanation: Plato described five perfect solids, built from flat faces that are all the same: cube, tetrahedron, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron.
Salt crystals grow as cubes, quartz as six-sided prisms, and many are other solids. Nature builds shapes that do not fit the four families.

explanations.art: Four trays labelled ball, box, tin and cone, each holding three everyday things of that shape.

explanations.context: In Stack It you tried to build a tower from balls, boxes, tins and a cone. This card says which shapes stack and why.
explanations.definition: A thing can go in the middle of a tower only if it has a flat face below and a flat face on top.
explanations.description: Put one matchbox on another. Flat face sits on flat face, and it stays. Now put a lemon on a lemon. They touch at one tiny spot, and the top lemon rolls off. A tin standing up has a flat face below and a flat face on top, so tins stack well. A cone has one flat face and a point. It can sit on top of a tower, but nothing can sit on its point.
examples: Shops stack soap boxes and tins on shelves.
Idli plates stack because each one is flat underneath.
Oranges are piled in a heap, not stacked in a straight tower.

perspectives.explanation: Made bricks all in one ratio, 1 to 2 to 4, so they stacked and bonded neatly in tall walls.
Build honeycomb from six-sided tubes that fit together with no gaps. Flat faces let them stack wax cells with the least wax.

explanations.art: A tower made of two matchboxes, then a round tin standing up, then a paper cone on top, with a lemon rolling away beside it.

explanations.concept: Why a cone rolls in a curve
explanations.context: In the Slope Test the tin rolled straight and the cone went round in a curve. This card says why.
explanations.definition: A tin is the same width at both ends, so it rolls straight. A cone is wide at one end and has a point at the other, so it rolls in a curve.
explanations.description: Lay a cone on the floor and push it gently. Watch the two ends. In one full turn, the wide end travels a long way round. The point hardly moves. So the cone swings round its point. Both ends of a tin are the same width, so both travel the same distance, and the tin goes straight. A tumbler that is wider at the top is in between, and it rolls in a big curve.
examples: A party cap pushed on the floor goes round its point.
A rolling pin rolls straight.
A paper cup rolls in a wide curve.
explanations.art: A paper cone on a floor with a curved chalk line showing its path round its point, next to a tin with a straight chalk line.

chart.title: How far each end goes in one turn of a cone

explanations.one_view: I asked about scale, scientists, traditions, other beings and history and found no second view. A cone is wider at one end, so one side travels further than the other and it turns in a circle. This is a geometry fact that anyone can test.

explanations.context: This card looks at the word for a tin shape in three languages. It shows that people often named this shape by what it does.
explanations.definition: A shape's name is a word people chose. For the tin shape, many people chose a word that means rolling.
explanations.description: The maths name for a tin shape is cylinder. It comes from an old Greek word, kylindros, which means roller. In Tamil the word urulai is used for this shape and for a wheel. It comes from urul, which means to roll. In Hindi the shape is called belan, which is also the rolling pin in the kitchen. So people far apart noticed the same thing about this shape: it rolls. But a tin also stands and stacks, and the names leave that out.
examples: English: cylinder, from the Greek word for roller.
Tamil: urulai, from urul, to roll.
Hindi: belan, the same word as a rolling pin.

perspectives.explanation: The word cylinder comes from kylindros, a Greek word linked to rolling. Sphere comes from sphaira, a ball. The names speak of what the shape does.
Call the same shape yuanzhu, which means round pillar. It names what the shape looks like, not how it moves.

explanations.art: A rolling pin in the middle with three word labels around it: cylinder, urulai and belan.

explanations.concept: Is a coin flat or solid?
explanations.context: A coin looks flat, but it rolled on its edge in the Slope Test. This card asks whether anything you can hold is really flat.
explanations.definition: Everything you can hold is a solid shape, even a very thin thing.
explanations.description: Look at a coin from the side. It has a little thickness. It has 2 flat round faces and a thin curved surface between them, so it is a very short tin. That is why it rolls on its edge. A sheet of paper has a tiny thickness too, so it is a very thin box. In everyday talk we call coins and paper flat. In maths, a truly flat shape has no thickness at all. You can draw one, but you cannot pick one up.
examples: A coin is a very short tin shape.
A sheet of paper is a very thin box shape.
A dosa is a short, wide tin shape, more or less.

perspectives.explanation: A coin is flat, so we call a circle on paper its shape.
A flat circle has no thickness. A real coin always has some thickness, so it is a very short solid tin shape.

explanations.art: A coin seen from the side, showing its thin edge, next to a tall round tin for comparison.

explanations.concept: Other living beings use solid shapes too
explanations.context: People are not the only ones who make things that roll and slide. This card gives two examples that scientists have watched closely.
explanations.definition: Many living beings make solid shapes and use the way those shapes move.
explanations.description: Some dung beetles feed on the dung of cows and elephants. A beetle pats a lump of dung into a ball. Then they walk backwards and push the ball away with their back legs. A ball rolls any way you push it, so the food is soon far from other beetles. Such beetles live in India too. A young antlion lives in dry sand. They dig a pit shaped like a cone, with the point at the bottom, and wait there. An ant who steps over the edge slides down the loose sand.
examples: A dung beetle shapes dung into a ball and rolls it away.
An antlion digs a cone-shaped pit in dry sand.
An Indian pangolin curls up into a ball when they are in danger.

perspectives.explanation: Honeybees build six-sided wax tubes so well that it looks like clever design that saves wax.
The wax warms and flows into hexagons by itself, like soap bubbles, so the bees do not need to calculate. Scientists still discuss how much is bee and how much is physics.

explanations.art: A dung beetle pushing a ball of dung backwards across dry ground, with a small cone-shaped pit in the sand nearby.

explanations.concept: Balls in the sky, boxes in the wall, tins under the bus
explanations.context: This card looks at where balls, boxes and tins turn up in the world, and gives a simple reason for each.
explanations.definition: Each solid shape turns up where its way of moving or staying is useful.
explanations.description: The Earth is a huge ball, and so are the Moon and the Sun. Told simply, each one pulls everything in it towards its middle, from every side. About 1,500 years ago the Indian mathematician Aryabhata wrote that the Earth is round. Bricks are box shapes, and their flat faces stack, so a wall stays up. A wheel is a short tin shape lying on its curved surface, and that is why a bus rolls. A wall that rolled would be no use, and nor would a bus that stayed. You will learn the fuller reasons in later years.
examples: The Earth, the Moon and the Sun are ball shapes.
Bricks are box shapes, so they stack into walls.
The wheels of a bus, a cycle and a suitcase are short tin shapes.

perspectives.explanation: Believed the heavens must be made of perfect spheres, because the sphere was the most perfect shape.
Say gravity pulls big things into a ball, because every part is drawn toward the centre. Small space rocks stay lumpy, like potatoes, because their gravity is too weak to round them.

explanations.art: A street scene with the full Moon above, a brick wall, and a bus whose wheels are drawn boldly.

agreed.text: A ball has no flat face anywhere, so it rolls whichever way you push it.
agreed.evidence: Run your palm over a ball. It never lies flat. On the slope in the Slope Test, the ball rolled however you put it down.

agreed.text: A box has only flat faces, so it cannot roll. On a steep slope it slides.
agreed.evidence: In the Slope Test the matchbox and the dice stayed on the gentle slope. On the steep slope they moved down with the same face on the tray.

agreed.text: A round tin can roll and can stay. It rolls on its curved side and stays on its flat end.
agreed.evidence: You tested the same tin both ways in the Slope Test. Nothing about the tin changed except the part that touched the tray.

agreed.text: Some dung beetles shape dung into a ball and roll it away in a straight line. On dark, clear nights they keep straight by the glow of the Milky Way.
agreed.evidence: In 2013 Marie Dacke and other scientists let beetles roll their balls under a real night sky and under a star show inside a dome. Under a cloudy sky, the beetles could not keep a straight path.

agreed.text: The Earth is a ball, even though the ground looks flat from where we stand.
agreed.evidence: Photographs taken from space show a ball from every side. Long before that, about 1,500 years ago, the Indian mathematician Aryabhata wrote that the Earth is round and turns.

challenging.claim: Every thing is either a roller or a slider.
challenging.who: Most of us, when we sort things into two heaps
challenging.context: This card is about sorting things into things that roll and things that slide. It shows that some things do not fit in one heap.
challenging.for: It works for many things. A ball always rolls. A matchbox never rolls. Two heaps are easy to remember.
challenging.against: A tin, a cone and a coin each roll one way up and slide another way up. So the two heaps are about the part that touches the ground, not about the whole thing.

challenging.who: Many young children, and grown-ups in everyday talk
challenging.context: This card is about the difference between a ball and a circle, which people often mix up.
challenging.for: Look at a ball from any side and its outline is a circle. We even say the Sun is a circle in the sky.
challenging.against: A circle is flat. You can draw it, but you cannot pick it up. A ball is solid. You can hold it, and it rolls. In maths the two have different names.

challenging.claim: A murre's pointed egg rolls in a circle, so that it does not fall off the cliff.
challenging.who: Many bird books, from the middle of the 1900s onwards
challenging.context: A murre is a seabird who lays one pointed egg on a bare cliff ledge. This card is about why the egg has that shape. Scientists do not agree.
challenging.for: A pointed egg does roll in a curve, as a cone does. On a wide, flat ledge that could keep it from the edge.
challenging.against: Tim Birkhead and his team measured the curve. It is often wider than the ledge, so the egg would still fall. In 2018 they found that pointed eggs sit more steadily on a slope. The shape may help the egg stay still.

big_questions.q: A tin rolls lying down and stays standing up. So is a tin a roller or not?
big_questions.hint: What changed when you stood it up? What did not change?

big_questions.q: Can you think of a solid shape that has no flat face and still cannot roll?
big_questions.hint: Think of a banana or a crumpled paper. Is it curved the same way all over?

big_questions.q: Why can you stack boxes but not balls?
big_questions.hint: Look at how much of each one touches the one below.

big_questions.q: You can draw a circle, but can you ever hold one in your hand?
big_questions.hint: Is a coin a circle? Look at it from the side.

big_questions.q: The Earth is a ball. So why does the ground look flat?
big_questions.hint: Think of an ant walking on a football.

big_questions.q: A dung beetle makes a ball without knowing the word 'ball'. What does the beetle know?
big_questions.hint: Do you need a word to know that a thing rolls?

story.title: The Blue Drum on the Hill Lane
story.note: Kani, Chithi, Babu and Stella teacher are made up. Coonoor is a real hill town in the Nilgiris of Tamil Nadu, with sloping lanes.
text: Friday was market day in Coonoor, and the lane to the market went uphill all the way.

Kani's Chithi had a stall on that lane. She sold everything a kitchen needs. There were steel tumblers and tiffin boxes. There were plastic balls for small children. And at the back, standing like a guard, there was one big blue drum for storing water.
"Can I help today?" asked Kani.
"You can set out the table," said Chithi. "Carrying is for big people." Babu anna was fourteen, and he did the carrying.
The table stood on the lane, so it leaned a little, like the lane.

Kani put six plastic balls in a row. Before she could count them, they ran off the low end of the table. They bounced, and then they rolled away down the lane. Babu ran after them. A goat watched him go.
Next Kani laid the tumblers down in a neat row, like children asleep. The tumblers rolled too. They rolled in a lazy curve, clinked into each other and dropped off the edge.
Kani sat down on an upturned crate and looked at the table for a while.
Then she tried the tiffin boxes. She set one down. It did not move. She set down another. It stayed where she had put it. She turned one over and looked underneath. It was flat. All of it was flat.
She picked up a tumbler. Its side was round, like the balls. But its bottom was flat, like the boxes.
She stood the tumbler up on its bottom. It stayed.

After that she worked fast. She stood every tumbler up, in rows of five. She built a little square wall out of tiffin boxes and tipped the balls inside it. The balls rolled as far as the wall and stopped.
Chithi came back with the tea and looked at the table. "Who showed you that?"
"The table did," said Kani.
At noon Stella teacher came by and bought the big blue drum. "Send it up soon," she said. "The water comes at one o'clock. I live in the last house at the top, with the green gate."
But Babu had gone to the bus stand with a parcel, and Chithi could not leave the stall.

Kani went and stood beside the drum. It was empty, so it was not heavy. But it came up to her chest, and it was far too wide to hug. She tried anyway. Her arms did not reach halfway round, and she could not see where she was going.
Carrying is for big people, she thought.
She looked at the drum again. It had a round side. It had a flat bottom and a flat lid.
"You are only a big tumbler," she told it.
She tipped the drum over on to its side. She put both hands on it and pushed. The drum rolled. It rolled up the lane, past the tea shop and past the tailor. People stepped aside to let it through.
Halfway up, Kani stopped to get her breath. She took her hands away.
The drum began to roll back down the lane, towards the stall and all the tumblers.
Kani ran round it. She pushed against it with her whole body. Then she heaved one end up, and up, until the drum stood on its flat bottom.
It stood on the slope as if it had always been there.
Kani sat down beside it and laughed. When she was ready, she laid it down again. She rolled it the rest of the way to the green gate and stood it up.
Stella teacher came out, wiping her hands. "Who carried this all the way up?"
"Nobody," said Kani. "It goes when it is lying down. It waits when it is standing up."
When she got back to the stall, Babu was there. He was tidying the table, and he was laying the tumblers down in a neat row.
"Not like that, anna," said Kani. "Let me show you."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kani finds that the balls and the lying tumblers roll off a sloping table, and the flat tiffin boxes stay. Then she sees that a tumbler has both a round side and a flat bottom, so she can choose what it does. She uses the same idea twice with the drum: she lays it down to move it and stands it up to stop it. A curved surface rolls and a flat face stays, and one thing can have both.
ask: Why did the balls run off the table when the tiffin boxes did not?
Kani told the drum, 'You are only a big tumbler.' What did she mean?
How did Kani stop the drum from rolling back down the lane?
If the drum had been a big box, how could Kani have moved it up the lane?

experiments.title: The Slope Test: which things roll and which slide?
experiments.context: In this test you build a slope from a tray and some books. First you guess what each thing will do. Then you let each one go at the top. You will find out what makes a thing roll and what makes it slide.
experiments.question: A ball, a round tin, a matchbox, a dice, a paper cone and a coin sit at the top of a slope. Which will roll, which will slide, and why?
experiments.predict: Before you let anything go, guess for each thing: will it roll, slide or stay? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every thing starts on the same line at the top. We let go without pushing. We use the same slope for all of them. We write the guess before the test, so the test cannot change the guess.
results_table: Thing, and how it is placed

materials.item: a smooth steel tray, a chopping board or a big hardbound book, for the slope
thick books to lift one end of the slope
a ball. A marble or a round lemon will also do
a round tin or dabba with straight sides and its lid on. A glue stick will also do
a matchbox
a dice
a paper cone. A party cap or an ice-cream cone will also do
a coin
a towel to catch things at the bottom, and paper and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the paper for the cone. Keep marbles, coins and dice away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Build the slope. Guess what each thing will do. Test on a gentle slope, then on a steep slope. Sort the things and say the rule.

experiments.record: A grown-up draws a table with four columns and eight rows. Write the guess first. Then write what happened on the gentle slope and on the steep slope: rolled, slid or stayed. At the end, the child says the rule and the grown-up writes it under the table.

flow.do: 1. Put 2 thick books under one end of the tray. 2. Draw a line across the top end. 3. Put a towel at the bottom. 4. Make the paper cone. 5. Lay the six things beside the slope.
flow.say: This is our slope. One end is high and one end is low. We will let each thing go from this line.
flow.kid: Build a slope with a tray and 2 books. Put the six things next to it.
flow.parent: For the cone, draw round a dinner plate on paper and cut the circle out. Fold it in half and cut along the fold. Roll one half into a cone and tape it. Use a smooth slope. A cloth cover grips too much.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Slope Test. You build a gentle slope and lay out six things to test.

flow.do: 1. Hold up each thing in turn. 2. Show how it will be placed. 3. Ask if it will roll, slide or stay, and why. 4. Write each guess. 5. Do not correct any guess.
flow.say: Will this one roll, slide or stay where it is? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess for each thing: roll, slide or stay? Say why.

ask.q: What will the tin do when it stands on its end? Why?
good: It will roll, because it is round.
It will stay, because the bottom is flat.

flow.parent: Many children say every round thing will roll, even the tin standing up and the coin lying flat. Accept each guess with its reason. The slope will do the correcting.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Slope Test. Before any testing, you guess what each of the six things will do on the slope.

flow.do: 1. Put the ball on the top line. 2. Let go without pushing. 3. Write what happened. 4. Do the same for all eight tests. 5. Lay the tin across the slope, not pointing down it.
flow.say: Put it on the line and just let go. What did it do? Did it turn over and over, or stay?
flow.kid: Put each thing on the line. Let go. Do not push. Watch what it does.

ask.q: Which things moved on the gentle slope? Which stayed?
good: The ball and the tin lying down rolled.
The cone went round in a curve.
The matchbox, the dice and the coin stayed.

flow.parent: On 2 books, the ball, the tin lying down and the cone lying down should move. The cone swings round its point and may stop. The rest should stay. If something flat slides already, take one book away.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the Slope Test. You test all six things on the gentle slope and write what each one did.

flow.do: 1. Add 3 more books to make the slope steep. 2. Test again each thing that stayed. 3. Ask your child to watch which face is on the tray. 4. Write what happened.
flow.say: Now the slope is steep. Watch the matchbox closely. Does it turn over, or does one face stay down?
flow.kid: Make the slope steep. Test the things that stayed. Do they turn over?

ask.q: The matchbox moved this time. Did it roll?
good: The same face stayed on the tray.

flow.parent: If a thing still stays, lift the high end slowly by hand until it moves. A tall thin tin may fall over when standing. Use a short one, or hold the slope a little lower.
flow.context: This is step 4 of the Slope Test. You make the slope steep and test again the things that stayed the first time.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to make two heaps: things that rolled and things that slid. 2. Hold up the tin and ask where it goes. 3. Your child runs a palm over each thing. 4. Ask what the rollers share.
flow.say: Make two heaps: rolled, and slid. Now, where does the tin go? Feel each thing with your palm.
flow.kid: Make two heaps: rolled, and slid. Where does the tin go? Feel each thing.

ask.q: The tin rolled lying down and slid standing up. Which heap is it in?
good: It needs to be in the middle.
It depends how you put it.

ask.q: Feel the ball and the matchbox. What is different?
good: The ball is curved all over.
My hand lies flat on the box but not on the ball.

check.q: A round tin stands on its flat end on a gentle slope. What will it do?
check.why: It stays. A flat face is on the slope, and a flat face does not roll. Picking 'roll down' means thinking a round thing always rolls. Check which part is touching the slope.

flow.parent: The tin, the cone and the coin do not fit in one heap. Let your child feel the puzzle before you help. Put them between the two heaps.
flow.context: This is step 5 of the Slope Test. You sort the things into rollers and sliders, and find one that belongs in both heaps.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they think makes a thing roll. 2. Ask what they saw that shows it. 3. Ask why. 4. Write their words under the table.
flow.say: What do you think makes a thing roll? What did you see? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Say what makes a thing roll. Say what makes a thing slide.

ask.q: What do you think now? What did you see? Why?
good: A thing rolls on its curved part.
A flat part slides or stays.
The tin did both, so it is about which part is down.
The matchbox never rolled, and it is flat all over.

check.q: Which thing can never roll, however you place it?
check.why: A matchbox. It has only flat faces, so it has no curved surface to roll on. A ball always rolls. A tin rolls when it lies on its side.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Slope Test. You say the rule you found for rolling and sliding.

activities.title: Stack It: which shapes can go in a tower?
activities.context: In this activity you try to build the tallest tower you can from boxes, tins, a cone and a ball. You will find out what a shape needs before another shape can sit on it.
activities.problem: You have 3 matchboxes, 2 round tins, 1 cone and 1 ball. How tall a tower can you build with all of them? Which ones cause trouble?

materials.item: matchboxes or soap boxes
round tins or dabbas with flat lids
a paper cone or party cap
a ball or a round lemon

schedule.what: Guess which shapes will stack. Build a tower. Try each shape at the bottom, in the middle and on top. Say the rule.

activities.record: Draw your tallest tower. Beside each shape write B for box, T for tin, C for cone. Write how many things are in it.

example_chart.title: Where each shape could go (your tower may differ)

setup.art: Three matchboxes, two round tins, a paper cone and a ball laid out on a floor.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the 7 things. Guess: which ones will stack?

setup.art: A child placing a round tin, standing up, on top of two stacked matchboxes.
setup.caption: 2. Build a tower. Use as many things as you can.

setup.art: A child trying to balance a matchbox on the point of a paper cone, the matchbox tipping off.
setup.caption: 3. Try the cone and the ball in the middle. What happens?

setup.art: A finished tower of three matchboxes and two tins with the cone on top, and the ball sitting on the floor beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Count your tower. Which thing is left out?

flow.do: 1. Lay out the 7 things. 2. Ask which ones will be easy to stack and which will be hard. 3. Ask why. 4. Write the guesses.
flow.say: We will build a tower with these. Which ones will stack well? Which will not? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the 7 things. Guess which will stack and which will not.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stack It. You guess which of the 7 things can go in a tower.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds the tallest tower they can. 2. Do not help with the order. 3. When something falls, ask what the two touching parts were.
flow.say: Build it as tall as you can. When something falls off, tell me which two parts were touching.
flow.kid: Build the tallest tower you can. Use as many things as you can.

ask.q: The ball fell off. What was touching what?
good: A curved part on a flat part.
Only a tiny bit of the ball was touching.

flow.parent: Tins may be laid on their sides at first, and then roll away. Let it happen. Your child will soon stand them up.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Stack It. You build a tower from boxes, tins, a cone and a ball.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to try the cone at the bottom, in the middle and on top. 2. Do the same with the ball. 3. Fill in yes or no in the table.
flow.say: Try the cone in three places: bottom, middle, top. Where does it work? Now try the ball.
flow.kid: Try the cone at the bottom, in the middle and on top. Then try the ball.

ask.q: Why can the cone go on top but not in the middle?
good: Its bottom is flat but its top is a point.
Nothing can sit on the point.

check.q: Which of these can go in the middle of a tower?
check.why: A tin standing up. It has a flat face below and a flat face on top. A ball has no flat face. A cone has a point on top, so nothing can sit on it.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Stack It. You test where the cone and the ball can go in a tower.

flow.do: 1. Count the things in the tallest tower. 2. Ask which thing was left out. 3. Ask your child for the rule.
flow.say: How many things are in your tower? Which one could not join? What does a thing need so that it can stack?
flow.kid: Count your tower. Which thing is left out? What does a shape need to stack?

ask.q: What does a shape need so that another can sit on it?
good: A flat face on top and one underneath.

flow.parent: The tallest tower uses 6 things: 3 boxes and 2 tins in any order, with the cone on top. The ball is left out.
flow.context: This is the last step of Stack It. You count your tower and say what a shape needs so that it can stack.

activities.title: The Feel Bag: name the shape without looking
activities.context: In this activity you put your hand into a cloth bag and feel one thing. You count its flat faces with your fingers and say its family before you pull it out. It shows that you can know a solid shape by touch alone.
activities.problem: Can you tell a ball, a box, a tin and a cone apart with your eyes shut? What do your fingers look for?

materials.item: a cloth bag or a pillow cover
small things: a marble or lemon, a matchbox, a dice, a glue stick or small round tin, a paper cone, a coin

activities.safety: Use only things with no sharp points or edges.

schedule.what: Feel one thing at a time in the bag. Say what your fingers find. Name the family. Pull it out and check.

activities.record: Make one tally stroke for each right guess. Write how many you got right out of 6.

rows: 1 flat round end and a point
example_chart.title: What fingers look for

setup.art: A parent dropping a matchbox, a marble, a glue stick and a paper cone into a cloth bag while the child looks away.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up puts 6 things in a bag. Do not look.

setup.art: A child with one arm deep in a cloth bag, eyes closed, thinking.
setup.caption: 2. Feel one thing. Is it flat, curved or both?

setup.art: A child pulling a glue stick out of the bag and smiling.
setup.caption: 3. Name the family. Pull it out and check.

flow.do: 1. Put the 6 things in the bag while your child looks away. 2. Say the four families aloud together.
flow.say: There are six things in this bag. Each one is a ball, a box, a tin or a cone. You will find out with your fingers.
flow.kid: Six things are hiding in the bag. Do not peep.

chart.title: Each thing is one of these

flow.context: This is the first step of the Feel Bag. A grown-up hides six things in a cloth bag.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts one hand in and holds one thing. 2. Ask if it has a flat face, and how many. 3. Ask if any part is curved. 4. Your child names the family, then pulls it out.
flow.say: Hold one thing. Can you find a flat face? How many? Is any part curved? Which family is it?
flow.kid: Hold one thing. Count its flat faces. Is any part curved? Name the family.

ask.q: It has 2 flat round ends and a curved side. What is it?

check.q: Your fingers find no flat face at all. Which family is it?
check.why: A ball. It is curved all over. A box has 6 flat faces and a cone has 1.

flow.parent: The coin is the hard one. It feels flat, but it has 2 flat faces and a thin curved edge, like a very short tin.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Feel Bag. You feel one thing at a time, count its flat faces and name its family.

flow.do: 1. Count the right guesses. 2. Ask which thing was hardest. 3. Swap: your child hides things for you.
flow.say: How many did you get right? Which one fooled your fingers? Now you hide some for me.
flow.kid: Count your right guesses. Which thing was hardest? Now hide some for a grown-up.

ask.q: Why is the coin hard to name?
good: It is like a tiny tin.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Feel Bag. You count your right guesses and then swap places.

activities.title: Maths in life: ball, rope and box from dough
activities.context: Cooks make solid shapes with their hands every day: laddus, seedai, chapati dough. In this activity you make a ball, a tin shape, a cone and a box from dough. You will find out which hand movement makes which shape, and why a rolling pin is the shape it is.
activities.problem: How do your hands have to move to make a ball? A tin shape? A box? And why is a rolling pin not a box?

materials.item: chapati dough or play dough, a lump as big as a lemon
a plate or chapati board
a rolling pin
a matchbox or small box

activities.safety: Wash hands first. If you will cook the dough afterwards, a grown-up does the cooking.

schedule.what: Make a ball, a tin shape, a cone and a box from dough. Test each on a tilted plate. Then roll dough flat with a rolling pin and with a box.

activities.record: Draw the four dough shapes. Under each, draw how your hands moved: round and round, back and forth, or pressing flat.

rows: round and round between two palms
back and forth on the board
back and forth, pressing one end more
example_chart.title: Hands and shapes

setup.art: A child rolling a lump of dough between two palms in a circular movement, a parent beside her doing the same.
setup.caption: 1. Roll dough round and round between your palms. What shape do you get?

setup.art: A child rolling a lump of dough back and forth on a chapati board with one flat hand, making a short thick rope.
setup.caption: 2. Roll dough back and forth on the board. What shape now?

setup.art: A child pressing a lump of dough against the board on each side in turn to make a box shape.
setup.caption: 3. Press a lump flat on six sides to make a box.

setup.art: A rolling pin rolling over dough on a board, with a matchbox sitting unused beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Roll dough flat with the rolling pin. Then try with a box.

flow.do: 1. Give your child a lump of dough. 2. Ask them to make a ball, any way they like. 3. Ask how their hands moved. 4. Make one yourself.
flow.say: Make me a ball. Now tell me, how did your hands move?
flow.kid: Make a ball from dough. How did your hands move?

ask.q: How did your hands move to make the ball?

flow.parent: A ball needs the palms to circle, so every side gets pressed the same. This is how laddus and seedai are shaped.

chart.title: Four dough shapes: ball, tin, cone, box

flow.context: This is the first step of the dough activity. You make a ball and notice how your hands moved.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a tin shape, like a short thick rope. 2. Ask how the hands moved this time. 3. Ask for a cone. 4. Ask what they did differently.
flow.say: Now make a tin shape, like a thick rope. How did your hands move this time? Now turn one into a cone.
flow.kid: Make a tin shape. Then make a cone. How did your hands move?

ask.q: What did you do to turn the tin shape into a cone?

flow.parent: Back and forth in one direction makes a tin shape. The dough only turns one way, so it stays the same width. Pat the two ends flat on the board.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the dough activity. You make a tin shape and a cone, and compare how your hands moved.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a box. 2. Let your child find out that rolling does not work. 3. Show pressing each side flat on the board. 4. Count the 6 faces together.
flow.say: Now make a box. Can you roll it? What do you have to do?
flow.kid: Make a box from dough. Can you roll it into shape? Count its faces.

ask.q: Why can you not make a box by rolling?
good: A box needs flat faces, so I have to press.

flow.context: This is step 3 of the dough activity. You make a box and find that it needs pressing, not rolling.

flow.do: 1. Tilt the plate a little. 2. Your child guesses what each dough shape will do. 3. Test all four. 4. Compare with the Slope Test.
flow.say: I will tilt the plate. What will each dough shape do? Why?
flow.kid: Tilt the plate. Guess what each dough shape will do. Then test.

check.q: You tilt the plate a little. Which dough shape stays where it is?
check.why: The box. It rests on a flat face. The ball and the rope each rest on a curved surface, so they roll.

flow.parent: Soft dough sticks a little, so tilt further than you did with the tray. Dust the plate with dry flour if nothing moves.
flow.context: This is step 4 of the dough activity. You test your four dough shapes on a tilted plate.

flow.do: 1. Press the ball a little flat. 2. Your child rolls it out with the rolling pin. 3. Then they try to roll it out with a matchbox. 4. Ask why the pin works.
flow.say: Roll the dough flat with the pin. Now try with the matchbox. Which works? Why?
flow.kid: Roll dough flat with the rolling pin. Then try with a box. Which works?

ask.q: Why is a rolling pin a tin shape?
good: Its curved side rolls over the dough.
A box only pushes the dough.

flow.parent: The pin's curved surface rolls over the dough and presses it evenly. A box can only slide and scrape. If you are making chapatis today, let your child roll one.
flow.context: This is the last step of the dough activity. You find out why a rolling pin is a tin shape and not a box.

activities.title: Maths in life: a rolling game and a sliding game
activities.context: Goli, the game of marbles, is a rolling game. Carrom is a sliding game: its coins slide on their flat faces. In this activity you roll a marble and slide a coin towards the same line and keep score. You will find out which is easier to send far and which is easier to stop where you want.
activities.problem: From the same start line, which gets closer to the target line: a marble that rolls or a coin that slides?

materials.item: a marble or small ball
a carrom coin or a flat coin
chalk or tape for two lines on a smooth floor
paper and a pencil for the score

activities.safety: Play on the floor, away from stairs. Keep marbles and coins away from babies and toddlers.

schedule.what: Mark a start line and a target line. Roll a marble 5 times and slide a coin 5 times. Score a point each time one stops within a hand of the target line.

activities.record: Make two rows on paper: marble and coin. Make one tally stroke for each try that stops within one hand of the target line.

example_chart.title: One family's score out of 5 (yours will differ)

setup.art: Two chalk lines on a smooth floor about two big steps apart, with a child kneeling behind the first line.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a start line and a target line, 2 big steps apart.

setup.art: A child rolling a marble along the floor towards the far chalk line.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the marble. Try to stop it near the target line.

setup.art: A child flicking a carrom coin with one finger so that it slides along the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Slide the coin with a flick, as in carrom.

setup.art: A hand laid flat on the floor between a coin and the chalk line to check the distance, with a tally sheet nearby.
setup.caption: 4. Within one hand of the line? Make a stroke.

flow.do: 1. Mark a start line on a smooth floor. 2. Mark a target line 2 big steps away. 3. Ask which will be easier to stop near the line, the marble or the coin, and why.
flow.say: We will send a marble and a coin to that line. Which will be easier to stop near it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw two lines. Guess: which stops nearer the line, the marble or the coin?
flow.context: This is the first step of the rolling and sliding game. You mark two lines and guess which thing is easier to stop near the target.

flow.do: 1. Your child rolls the marble from the start line, 5 times. 2. After each try, check with a flat hand. 3. Make a stroke if it stopped within one hand of the line.
flow.say: Roll it gently. Did it stop within one hand of the line? If yes, make a stroke.
flow.kid: Roll the marble 5 times. Make a stroke each time it stops near the line.

ask.q: What does the marble do after it passes the line?

flow.parent: A marble keeps rolling on a smooth floor, so it often runs far past the line. That is the point of this step.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the rolling and sliding game. You roll a marble 5 times and score each try.

flow.do: 1. Your child slides the coin from the start line with a finger flick, 5 times. 2. Check each try with a flat hand. 3. Make a stroke for each near try.
flow.say: Now flick the coin so that it slides. Did it stop within one hand of the line?
flow.kid: Slide the coin 5 times. Make a stroke each time it stops near the line.

ask.q: The coin stopped sooner than the marble. Why might that be?
good: The floor grips its flat face.
Its whole face rubs on the floor.

flow.parent: A sliding coin rubs the floor with its whole face, so it slows down quickly. A carrom board is dusted with powder to make the coins slide further.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the rolling and sliding game. You slide a coin 5 times and score each try.

flow.do: 1. Count the strokes in each row. 2. Ask which was easier to send far. 3. Ask which was easier to stop near the line.
flow.say: Count the strokes. Which went further on a small push? Which was easier to stop near the line?
flow.kid: Count your strokes. Which went further? Which was easier to stop?

check.q: On a smooth floor, which usually goes further on the same small push?
check.why: The marble. A rolling thing touches the floor at a tiny spot. A sliding coin rubs the floor with its whole face and slows down sooner.

flow.parent: Scores differ from floor to floor. Most families find the marble goes further and the coin is easier to place. In a cricket match, the ball rolls all the way to the boundary for the same reason.
flow.context: This is the last step of the rolling and sliding game. You compare the scores of the marble and the coin.

activities.title: Everyone does maths: push like a dung beetle
activities.context: A dung beetle shapes food into a ball and rolls it away. In this activity you push a ball and a box across the floor with one finger and count the pushes. You will find out why a ball is a good shape for moving food.
activities.problem: You must move a ball and a box from one line to another with one finger. Which needs fewer pushes? Which is easier to keep straight?

materials.item: a ball or a round lemon
a small box, about the same size as the ball
chalk or tape for two lines, 4 big steps apart

schedule.what: Guess which needs fewer pushes. Push the ball, then the box, from line to line with one finger. Count the pushes. Hear what dung beetles do.

activities.record: Write two numbers: pushes for the ball and pushes for the box.

setup.art: Two chalk lines on a floor about four steps apart, with a ball and a small box on the first line.
setup.caption: 1. Draw two lines, 4 big steps apart. Put the ball and the box on the first line.

setup.art: A child crouching and pushing a ball along the floor with one finger.
setup.caption: 2. Push the ball to the far line with one finger. Count the pushes.

setup.art: The same child pushing a small box along the floor with one finger, looking as if it is hard work.
setup.caption: 3. Now push the box. Count again.

flow.do: 1. Mark two lines 4 big steps apart. 2. Put the ball and the box on the first line. 3. Ask which will need fewer pushes, and why.
flow.say: You can use only one finger. Which will need fewer pushes to reach that line? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess: which needs fewer pushes, the ball or the box?
flow.context: This is the first step of the dung beetle activity. You guess whether a ball or a box needs fewer pushes to cross the floor.

flow.do: 1. Your child pushes the ball to the far line with one finger. 2. Count each push aloud. 3. Do the same with the box. 4. Write both numbers.
flow.say: Push and let go. That is one. Push again. Keep counting until it crosses the line.
flow.kid: Push the ball with one finger. Count your pushes. Then push the box.

ask.q: What happened to the ball between your pushes?
good: It went the wrong way a little.

check.q: A ball crossed the floor in 3 pushes. A box needed 14. Which needed more pushes?
check.why: The box. 14 is more than 3. The box slides and stops at once, so it needs a push for every little bit of the way.

flow.context: This is step 2 of the dung beetle activity. You count the pushes a ball needs and the pushes a box needs.

flow.do: 1. Read the dung beetle note to your child. 2. Ask why a beetle might make a ball and not a box. 3. Ask what the hard part of pushing a ball was.
flow.say: Some beetles shape dung into a ball and roll it away. Why a ball, do you think? What was hard about pushing yours?
flow.kid: A dung beetle rolls a ball of food away. Why a ball and not a box?

ask.q: Why might a beetle make a ball and not a box?
good: It rolls any way you push it.

flow.parent: Dung beetle note: the beetle walks backwards and pushes the ball with their back legs. A ball also wanders off line, as your child found. Scientists found that the beetles keep a straight path by looking at the sky: the Sun or the Moon, and on dark nights the glow of the Milky Way.
flow.context: This is the last step of the dung beetle activity. You think about why a dung beetle makes a ball.

games.title: Roll, Slide or Both?
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a dice game. Each roll names a family of solid shapes. You fetch a real thing of that family, say what it will do on the slope, and test it. It builds quick naming and quick thinking about rolling and sliding.

printables.title: A bowl of beans or buttons, about 20
items: One bean for each right call

rules: Keep the slope from the Slope Test, on 2 books. Put 20 beans in a bowl.
On your turn, roll the dice and read the key.
Fetch one thing of that shape from the room. It must be a thing nobody has used yet in this game.
Show how you will place it. Then call out: roll, slide or stay.
Test it on the slope. If your call was right, take a bean.
If you cannot find a thing of that shape in the time it takes to count to 20, you miss the turn.
The first player with 5 beans wins.
Playing alone: count how many turns you need to win 5 beans. Play again and try to need fewer.

setup.art: A tray propped on two books as a slope, a dice, a bowl of beans and a card showing the dice key.
setup.caption: 1. Set up the slope, the dice, the beans and the key.

setup.art: A child holding up a glue stick beside a dice showing 3, about to lay it on the slope.
setup.caption: 2. Roll. Fetch a thing of that shape. Call: roll, slide or stay.

setup.art: A glue stick rolling down the slope while the child takes one bean from the bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Test it. Right call? Take a bean.

flow.do: 1. Set the slope on 2 books. 2. Put 20 beans in a bowl. 3. Copy the dice key where everyone can see it.
flow.say: The dice tells you which shape to fetch. You say what it will do. The slope tells us if you are right.
flow.kid: Set up the slope and the beans. Read the dice key.
flow.context: This is the first step of Roll, Slide or Both?, a dice game. You set up the slope and read the dice key.

flow.do: 1. Play one practice turn. 2. Show that the way you place a tin changes the call. 3. Agree that the player chooses how to place it.
flow.say: I rolled a 3, so I fetch a tin shape. I will stand it up. My call is: stay. Let us test.
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Fetch the shape. Say how you will place it. Make your call.

check.q: You lay a glue stick on its side across a gentle slope. What is the right call?
check.why: Roll. Its curved surface is on the slope. If you stood it on its flat end, the right call would be stay.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Roll, Slide or Both?, a dice game. You practise one turn and see that how you place a thing changes what it does.

flow.do: 1. Play the game. 2. Each player says the family and the call aloud before testing. 3. Now and then, ask how many more beans a player needs.
flow.say: You have 3 beans. How many more do you need to reach 5?
flow.kid: Play the game. Say your call out loud before you test.

ask.q: You have 3 beans and you need 5. How many more?

flow.parent: Cones are hard to find. A funnel, a party cap, a sharpened pencil tip or a paper cone all count. Things that fit no family, such as a spoon, cannot be used.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Roll, Slide or Both?, a dice game. You play, and test each call on the slope.

flow.do: 1. The game ends when one player has 5 beans. 2. Ask which thing surprised everyone.
flow.say: Who reached 5 beans first? Which thing did something we did not expect?
flow.kid: The first player with 5 beans wins. Which thing surprised you?
flow.context: This is the last step of Roll, Slide or Both?, a dice game. You finish and say which thing surprised you.

games.title: Who Am I? Solid shape riddles
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a card game with 12 riddles. Each card gives a clue about a solid shape. You name the family, touch a thing of that shape in the room, and turn the card over to check.

printables.title: 12 riddle cards, with the clue on the front and the family on the back

items.f: I am curved all over. I have no flat face.
I have 6 flat faces. I never roll.
I have 2 flat round faces and a curved side.
I have 1 flat round face and a point.
Lay me down and I roll straight. Stand me up and I stay.
Push me on the floor and I go round my own point.
I roll whichever way you push me.
Many of me stack into a wall.
A rolling pin has my shape.
I can sit on top of a tower, but nothing can sit on me.

rules: Shuffle the 12 cards. Put them in a pile with the clues facing up.
On your turn, read the top clue aloud, or ask a grown-up to read it.
Name the family: ball, box, tin or cone. Then touch something in the room that has that shape.
Turn the card over to check. If you are right, keep the card. If not, put it at the bottom of the pile.
When the pile is gone, the player with the most cards wins.
Playing alone: count how many cards you get right the first time. Play again and try to beat your number.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards, or write them on slips of paper with the answer on the back. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Put them in a pile, clues up.
flow.say: Each card is a riddle from a solid shape. Listen to the clue and tell me who is talking.
flow.kid: Shuffle the cards. Put them in a pile with the clues facing up.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Am I?, a riddle card game about solid shapes. You make and shuffle the 12 cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. Read the top clue aloud. 3. The player names the family and touches one in the room. 4. Turn the card over to check.
flow.say: Here is the clue. Who am I? Now find me somewhere in this room.
flow.kid: Read the clue. Say the family. Touch that shape in the room. Then check.

check.q: Clue: 'Lay me down and I roll straight. Stand me up and I stay.' Who am I?
check.why: A tin. It rolls on its curved side and stays on its flat end. A ball cannot be stood up. A box never rolls.

flow.parent: If there is no cone in the room, a cone drawn in the air or the tip of a sharpened pencil counts.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Who Am I?, a riddle card game about solid shapes. You name the family from its clue and find it in the room.

flow.do: 1. When the pile is gone, count each player's cards. 2. Ask which clue was the hardest.
flow.say: How many cards do you have? Which clue was the hardest?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Which clue was the hardest?
flow.context: This is the last step of Who Am I?, a riddle card game about solid shapes. You count your cards and say which clue was hardest.

projects.title: My Solid Shape Shelf: five days, four families
projects.context: In this five-day project you make a small show of solid shapes on a shelf or a tray. Each day you collect things of one family. On the last day you look for things that fit no family at all.
projects.problem: Which family of solid shapes is easiest to find at home? Which is hardest? And what about the things that fit none?

materials.item: a shelf, a tray or a cardboard box lid
4 paper labels: ball, box, tin, cone
paper and a pencil for the count

projects.safety: Ask before you take things from the kitchen. Leave glass and sharp things where they are.

schedule.what: Ball day. Find 3 ball shapes. Feel each one: is any part flat? Put them by the ball label, in a bowl so they stay.
Box day. Find 3 box shapes of different sizes. Count the 6 faces of each. Stack them by the box label.
Tin day. Find 3 tin shapes: one tall, one short, one very thin like a coin. Stand them by the tin label.
Cone day. Find or make 2 cones. Stand them on their flat faces by the cone label.
Odd day. Find 3 things that fit no family. Count how many things each family has. Say which was hardest to find.

projects.record: On the last day, write the four family names and the number of things you found for each. Draw one thing that fits no family.

setup.art: A low shelf with four paper labels reading ball, box, tin and cone, and nothing else on it yet.
setup.caption: 1. Put four labels on a shelf or tray.

setup.art: A child placing a marble and a lemon in a small bowl beside the ball label.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, find things of one family.

setup.art: The shelf with three stacked boxes, three standing tins of different heights and two cones on it.
setup.caption: 3. Stack or stand them. Balls need a bowl.

setup.art: A child holding a spoon and a banana, looking at the four labels, unsure where they go.
setup.caption: 4. On the last day, find things that fit no family.

flow.do: 1. Write the four labels and put them on the shelf. 2. Your child finds 3 ball shapes. 3. They feel each one for flat parts. 4. Put the balls in a bowl by the label.
flow.say: Today is ball day. Find three. Feel each one. Is any part of it flat?
flow.kid: Find 3 ball shapes at home. Feel each one. Put them in a bowl.

ask.q: Why do the balls need a bowl?
good: They have no flat face to sit on.

flow.parent: A lemon or an orange is close to a ball but not exact. That is fine. Say 'nearly a ball'.
flow.context: This is day 1 of My Solid Shape Shelf, a five-day project. Today you find ball shapes and feel them for flat parts.

flow.do: 1. Your child finds 3 box shapes of different sizes. 2. They touch and count the 6 faces of each. 3. Stack them by the box label.
flow.say: Today is box day. Find a big one, a middle one and a small one. Count the faces of each.
flow.kid: Find 3 box shapes. Count the faces of each. Stack them up.
flow.wait: Do this on the next day
flow.context: This is day 2 of My Solid Shape Shelf, a five-day project. Today you find box shapes and count their 6 flat faces.

flow.do: 1. Your child finds 3 tin shapes: one tall, one short, one very thin. 2. They find the 2 flat faces of each. 3. Stand them by the tin label.
flow.say: Today is tin day. Find a tall one, a short one and a very thin one. Where are its two flat faces?
flow.kid: Find 3 tin shapes: tall, short and very thin. Stand them up.
flow.wait: Do this on the next day
flow.parent: The very thin one can be a coin, a bangle box lid or a carrom coin. It still has 2 flat faces and a curved edge.

rows.label: day 3: tins, seen from the side

flow.context: This is day 3 of My Solid Shape Shelf, a five-day project. Today you find tin shapes of different heights.

flow.do: 1. Look for cones together: a funnel, a party cap, an ice-cream cone. 2. If you find none, make 2 paper cones. 3. Stand them on their flat faces.
flow.say: Today is cone day. They are hard to find. Shall we look, and then make some?
flow.kid: Find or make 2 cones. Stand them on their flat faces.
flow.wait: Do this on the next day

rows.label: day 4: cones, seen from the side

flow.context: This is day 4 of My Solid Shape Shelf, a five-day project. Today you find or make cones.

flow.do: 1. Your child finds 3 things that fit no family. 2. Ask why each one does not fit. 3. Count the things in each family. 4. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Today is odd day. Find three things that are not a ball, a box, a tin or a cone. Why do they not fit?
flow.kid: Find 3 things that fit no family. Then count each family on your shelf.
flow.wait: Do this on the next day

ask.q: Why is a spoon not in any family?
good: It has a curved part but it is not a ball or a tin.

flow.parent: Most things in a home fit none of the four families exactly. The families are four simple shapes that people picked out because they are easy to describe.
flow.context: This is day 5 of My Solid Shape Shelf, a five-day project. Today you find things that fit no family and count your shelf.

challenges.title: Stretch: the cup that will not roll straight
challenges.context: This is a puzzle challenge that goes past Class 1. A paper cup is wider at the top than at the bottom. You roll it, mark its path, and then try to build something from two cups that rolls straight.
challenges.problem: A tin rolls straight. A paper cup rolls in a curve. Find out which way it curves and why. Then make two paper cups roll in a straight line together.
constraints: Roll on a flat floor, not on a slope.
Push gently, once, and let go.
For the last part you may use only 2 paper cups and tape.
materials: 2 paper cups of the same size, wider at the top. Steel tumblers that are wider at the top will do for the first part
a round tin with straight sides
chalk, or small bits of paper to mark the path
general: Roll the cup and watch which end travels further.
Mark where the cup is after each push, to see the curve.
Compare it with the tin, which goes straight.
creative: Tape two cups together bottom to bottom. The shape now rests on two wide rims of the same size, and it rolls straight.
Tape two cups together mouth to mouth. It rests on the join in the middle, tips to one side and curves again.
Put one cup inside the other. It still curves, because one end is still wider.
challenges.your_turn: Now make two paper cones: a short one and a long one, measured from the point to the rim. Roll each on the floor. Which goes round in the smaller circle? Guess first, then test.

setup.art: A paper cup lying on its side on a floor beside a round tin, with a child about to push the cup.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a paper cup and a tin on the floor. Guess the path of each.

setup.art: A paper cup rolling in a curve on a floor, with small bits of paper marking where it has been.
setup.caption: 2. Push the cup gently. Mark its path.

setup.art: Two paper cups taped together bottom to bottom, lying on their side.
setup.caption: 3. Tape two cups together. Can you make them roll straight?

setup.art: A short paper cone and a long paper cone side by side on the floor.
setup.caption: 4. Make a short cone and a long cone. Which makes the smaller circle?

flow.do: 1. Lay the tin and the cup on their sides. 2. Ask your child to guess the path of each. 3. Roll the tin first. 4. Then roll the cup and watch.
flow.say: The tin and the cup both have a curved side. Will they roll the same way? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how the tin will roll. Guess how the cup will roll. Then test.

ask.q: What did the cup do that the tin did not?

flow.parent: The cup curves towards its narrow end. Many children expect it to roll straight, like the tin.
flow.context: This is the first step of the cup challenge. You compare how a tin and a paper cup roll on a flat floor.

flow.do: 1. Roll the cup again, slowly. 2. Put a bit of paper where the wide end is after each push. 3. Do the same for the narrow end. 4. Look at the two lines of paper.
flow.say: Let us mark where each end goes. Which end made the bigger curve?
flow.kid: Roll the cup slowly. Mark where the wide end goes. Mark the narrow end too.

ask.q: Which end travelled further?
good: The big end made the bigger circle.

check.q: A paper cup rolls on the floor. Which way does it curve?
check.why: Towards its narrow end. In one turn the wide end travels further than the narrow end, so the cup swings round the narrow side.

flow.parent: The two paper trails are parts of two circles, one inside the other. The wide end is on the outside.

chart.title: How far each end goes in one turn of the cup

flow.context: This is step 2 of the cup challenge. You mark the path of each end of the rolling cup.

flow.do: 1. Give your child 2 cups and tape. 2. Ask them to join the cups so that they roll straight. 3. Let them try more than one way. 4. Test each on the floor.
flow.say: Here are two cups and some tape. Can you join them so that they roll straight? Guess first, then try.
flow.kid: Join 2 cups with tape. Make them roll in a straight line.

ask.q: Why does it roll straight now?
good: It rolls on two rims that are the same size.
Each end goes the same distance.
One cup wants to turn one way and the other turns it back.

flow.parent: Bottom to bottom works: the shape rolls on its two wide rims. Mouth to mouth does not: it tips on to one cup and curves. Let your child try both. Help with the tape.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the cup challenge. You join two paper cups so that they roll straight.

flow.do: 1. Make a short cone and a long cone from paper. 2. Ask which will go round in the smaller circle. 3. Roll each. 4. Compare.
flow.say: One cone is short. One is long. Which will turn in the smaller circle? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make a short cone and a long cone. Which turns in the smaller circle?

ask.q: What did you notice about the long cone's circle?
good: The long cone needs more room to turn.

flow.parent: A cone turns round its own point, so a longer cone sweeps a bigger circle. For a short cone use half of a saucer-sized paper circle. For a long one use half of a dinner-plate circle. A grown-up cuts the paper.

chart.title: Which turns in the smaller circle?

flow.context: This is the last step of the cup challenge. You compare the circles made by a short cone and a long cone.

items.p: Which of these is a solid shape?
items.why: A ball. You can hold it, and it takes up room. A circle and a line on paper are flat.

items.p: Which one has no flat face?
items.why: The ball. It is curved all over. A box has 6 flat faces and a tin has 2.

items.p: A matchbox has ____ flat faces.
items.why: Top, bottom, front, back and two ends. That makes 6. Touch each one as you count.

items.p: A ball can roll whichever way you push it.
items.why: True. A ball is curved all over, so any side of it can roll.

items.p: Each thing sits on a steep slope. Will it roll or slide?
items.why: The marble, the football and the lemon rest on a curved surface, so they roll. The book, the matchbox and the dice rest on a flat face, so they slide.

items.p: Match each thing to its family.
items.why: A laddu is curved all over. A brick has 6 flat faces. A rolling pin has a curved side and 2 flat ends. A party cap has a point.

items.p: The squares are boxes and the circles are balls. There are ____ boxes.
items.why: Count the squares: 1, 2, 3. The two circles are balls.

items.p: A matchbox rolls down a gentle slope.
items.why: False. A matchbox has only flat faces. It stays on a gentle slope and slides on a steep one. It never rolls.

items.p: A tin lies on its side on a slope. What does it do?
items.why: It rolls. Its curved surface is on the slope.

items.p: Draw a tower of 2 boxes with a cone on top.
items.a: Two box shapes one above the other, with a pointed cone sitting on the top box.
items.why: The boxes have flat faces above and below, so they stack. The cone sits on its flat face, with its point up.

items.p: Draw one thing that rolls and one thing that slides. Write R on the roller and S on the slider.
items.a: A thing with a curved surface marked R, such as a ball, and a thing with flat faces marked S, such as a box.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the roller resting on a curved part and the slider resting on a flat face.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. Why does a ball roll when a matchbox does not?
items.a: A ball is curved all over. A matchbox has only flat faces.
items.why: A strong answer talks about the curved surface and the flat faces. It does not say 'because it is a ball'.

items.p: A round tin has ____ flat faces.

rows.label: a tin, seen from the side

items.why: The lid and the bottom. The side between them is curved.

items.p: A cone has ____ flat face.
items.why: Only the round bottom is flat. The other end is a point.

items.p: A tin standing on its flat end rolls down a gentle slope.
items.why: False. A flat face is on the slope, so the tin stays. It rolls only when it lies on its curved side.

items.p: A coin lies flat on a steep slope. What does it do?
items.why: It slides. Its flat face is on the slope. A coin rolls only when it is on its edge.

items.p: Put these in order, fewest flat faces first.
items.why: A ball has 0 flat faces. A cone has 1. A tin has 2. A box has 6.

items.p: Can it go in the middle of a tower?
items.why: The matchbox, the tin and the book each have a flat face below and on top. The lemon and the marble have no flat face. The party cap has a point on top.

items.p: Which thing can roll, and can also stand still on a slope?
items.why: A glue stick. It rolls on its curved side and stands on its flat end. A ball only rolls. A dice never rolls.

items.p: A tower has 3 boxes and 2 tins. How many things are in it? ____
items.why: 3 and 2 more make 5.

items.p: A round tin sits on the table.

views.says: A tin is a roller. Its side is round.
A tin is a stayer. I stand mine up and it never moves.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer says both are right about one way of placing the tin. It rolls lying down and stays standing up.
items.why: The tin has a curved side and two flat ends. What it does depends on which part is on the table.

items.p: Draw a tin lying down and a tin standing up. Colour the part that touches the floor.
items.a: Two tins. On the lying one a line along the curved side is coloured. On the standing one the flat bottom is coloured.
items.why: The lying tin touches the floor with its curved surface, so it rolls. The standing tin touches with a flat face, so it stays.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. Why can nothing sit on top of a cone?
items.a: The top of a cone is a point. There is no flat face to sit on.
items.why: A strong answer says that stacking needs a flat face on top, and a cone has only a point there.

items.p: Match each thing to what it does on a gentle slope.
pairs: rolls any way it is put
items.why: The ball is curved all over. The cone turns round its point. The matchbox rests on a flat face.

items.p: 2 matchboxes have ____ flat faces altogether.
items.why: Each matchbox has 6 flat faces. 6 and 6 make 12.

items.p: A tin and a cone together have ____ flat faces.
items.why: A tin has 2 flat faces and a cone has 1. 2 and 1 make 3.

items.p: A paper cup is wider at the top. How does it roll on the floor?
items.why: In a curve. The wide end travels further in one turn than the narrow end, so the cup swings round.

items.p: A coin is a very short tin shape.
items.why: True. A coin has 2 flat round faces and a thin curved surface between them, just like a tin.

items.p: Put these towers in order, fewest things first.
items.why: 2 boxes is 2 things. 1 box and 2 tins is 3 things. 4 boxes is 4 things.

items.p: You can see only a flat round face. Which thing can it NOT be?
items.why: A box. All the faces of a box have straight sides and corners. A tin and a cone each have a flat round face.

items.p: Tin shape or box shape?
items.why: The coin, the candle and the drum each have 2 flat round faces and a curved side. The book, the brick and the dice each have 6 flat faces.

items.p: Two cones can stack point to point.
items.why: False. A point is not a flat face. The top cone has nothing to rest on, and it falls.

items.p: A marble crossed the floor in 3 pushes. A box needed 9. The box needed ____ more pushes.
items.why: 9 take away 3 is 6. The box slides and stops, so it needs more pushes.

items.p: A cone is pushed on the floor. Draw its path. Mark where its point is.
items.a: A curved path or a circle, with the point of the cone at the middle of the circle.
items.why: A cone turns round its own point. The wide end travels round and the point stays nearly still.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. A dung beetle rolls food away as a ball. Why not as a box?
items.a: A ball rolls, so it is easy to push a long way. A box only slides and stops.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the pushing test showed: a ball needs far fewer pushes than a box.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. Is a sheet of paper flat or solid? Say why.
items.a: It is solid, but very thin. A pile of sheets shows the thickness.
items.why: A strong answer says that paper has a tiny thickness, so it is a very thin box. 'Flat' is how we speak of it every day.

quiz.p: Which of these can you pick up and hold?
quiz.why: A ball. It is a solid shape. The circle and the square are flat shapes drawn on paper.

quiz.p: Run your palm all over a matchbox. What do you feel?
quiz.why: Only flat faces. A matchbox has 6 of them and no curved surface.

quiz.p: How many flat faces does a ball have? ____
quiz.why: None. A ball is curved all over. Your palm cannot lie flat on it anywhere.

quiz.p: Which one will NOT roll on a gentle slope?
quiz.why: The box. It rests on a flat face, so it stays. The ball and the tin lying down rest on a curved surface, so they roll.

opts: It rests on a curved surface
quiz.why: It rests on a curved surface. A big football rolls too, so size is not the reason. A glass cube would not roll.

quiz.p: A brick is in which family?
quiz.why: Box. A brick has 6 flat faces and no curved surface.

quiz.p: A rolling pin is in which family?
quiz.why: Tin. It has a curved side and 2 flat round ends.

quiz.p: You want to put a box on top. Which thing can hold it?
quiz.why: A tin standing up. Its top is a flat face. A ball has no flat face, and a cone has a point on top.

quiz.p: You can stack lemons into a tall straight tower.
quiz.why: False. A lemon has no flat face. One lemon on another touches at a tiny spot and rolls off.

quiz.p: A glue stick stands on its flat end on a gentle slope. What does it do?
quiz.why: It stays. A flat face is on the slope. It would roll if you laid it on its curved side.

quiz.p: A coin stands on its edge. Then it lies flat. What has changed?
opts: The part that touches the floor
quiz.why: The part that touches the floor. On its edge the coin can roll. On its flat face it can only slide. The coin is the same.

quiz.p: A box has 6 flat faces. A tin has 2. How many altogether? ____
