applications: A cook rolls dough flat with a rolling pin. The pin is a tin shape, so its curved side rolls over the dough.
A mason builds a wall from bricks. Bricks are box shapes, so their flat faces stack.
Wheels on a bus, a cycle and a suitcase are short tin shapes that roll on their curved sides.
A shopkeeper stands tins and bottles on their flat ends, so that they stay on the shelf.
A road roller has a huge, heavy tin shape in front. It rolls over the road and presses it flat.
A carrom player slides a coin on its flat face. A cricket bowler sends a ball that rolls and bounces.
Workers lay a heavy drum on its side and roll it, which is easier than carrying it.
A funnel is a cone with the point cut off. Rice or oil slides down its sloping side into a narrow jar.

open_questions.q: Why is a murre's egg pointed at one end?
open_questions.why_open: For a long time people said it was so that the egg rolls in a circle. Tests in 2017 and 2018 pointed to other reasons, such as sitting steadily on a slope. Scientists are still studying it.

open_questions.q: What does a dung beetle sense when they pat dung into a ball?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can film the beetle and measure the ball. Nobody has found a way to ask the beetle what they are aiming for.

open_questions.q: Is there a perfect ball anywhere?
open_questions.why_open: Every ball people have made has tiny bumps. Even the Earth is a little wider round its middle. Nobody knows whether a perfect ball exists outside our minds.

open_questions.q: What does an antlion sense to get the slope of their pit right?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have watched how antlions dig, walking backwards and flicking sand out. What tells the antlion that the slope is steep enough is still being studied.

Is your tumbler a roller or a stayer right now? Can you make it the other one?
Why are wheels not box shapes?
Which things in the fridge are stacked? Which cannot be stacked?
Can you find a cone anywhere in this room?

jokes.j: Why does a cone never get lost?

jokes.j: What did the matchbox say to the marble?

jokes.j: Why did the ball not sit at the top of the tower?
jokes.a: It could not find a flat place to sit.

maths.problem: Kavya builds a tower with 3 matchboxes and 2 tins. She puts 1 cone on top. How many things are in her tower?
maths.explain: 3 matchboxes and 2 tins make 5. 1 cone more makes 6. So the tower has 6 things.
maths.context: In Stack It you built a tower from boxes, tins and a cone. Here you count the things in a tower without building it.

maths.problem: On a gentle slope, 3 tests rolled and 5 tests stayed. How many more stayed than rolled?
maths.explain: 5 stayed and 3 rolled. 5 take away 3 is 2. So 2 more stayed than rolled.
maths.context: In the Slope Test you wrote down what each thing did on the gentle slope. This uses one family's results.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers shows that most things do not roll, unless they rest on a curved part.

maths.problem: In the bag are 1 box, 1 tin and 1 cone. How many flat faces can your fingers find altogether?
maths.explain: The box has 6 flat faces. The tin has 2. The cone has 1. 6 and 2 make 8, and 1 more makes 9.
maths.context: In the Feel Bag you counted the flat faces of each thing with your fingers. Here you add the counts for three things.
maths.why_maths: Each family has its own number of flat faces. Adding them is a quick check that you know all three.

maths.problem: A tower goes box, tin, box, tin from the bottom up. What is the 6th thing? Could a cone be the 3rd thing?
maths.answer: The 6th thing is a tin. A cone cannot be the 3rd thing.
maths.explain: Box and tin take turns. The 1st, 3rd and 5th are boxes. The 2nd, 4th and 6th are tins. A cone has a point on top, so nothing could sit on it. It can only be the last thing.
maths.context: In Stack It you found where each shape can go in a tower. Here a tower follows a pattern.
maths.why_maths: Seeing the pattern tells you what comes next in the tower. Knowing the shapes tells you what cannot.

maths.problem: Meenu feels a thing in the bag. It has a flat round face. Is it surely a tin? What must she check?
maths.answer: Not surely. She must feel the other end.
maths.explain: A tin has a flat round face. So does a cone. Meenu must feel the other end. If there is a second flat round face, it is a tin. If there is a point, it is a cone.
maths.context: In the Feel Bag you named things by touch. This asks what one clue can and cannot tell you.
maths.why_maths: Knowing which clue is missing saves you from calling every round face a tin.

roots.context: We tested which things roll and which slide. Now let us think about the tin, which did both.

deep_truth.truth: In the Slope Test, the tin went into two heaps. Lying on its side, it rolled, and standing on its end, it stayed. It was the same tin. So a thing is not just a roller or a slider. It depends on which part of it meets the ground.
deep_truth.habit: We like to give every thing one label: this is a roller, that is a slider. The tin shows that one label is not enough. The two heaps were our idea, made to keep things simple.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Slope Test, the same tin rolled when its curved surface was on the tray and stayed when its flat face was on the tray. The cone and the coin did the same.

three.who_am_i: You made the heaps. You could have sorted the same things by colour or by size. You chose to sort by how they move.
three.what_is_life: A dung beetle has never done a slope test. They still pat their food into a ball, and a ball is the shape that rolls best.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth under your feet is a huge ball. From where you stand, the ground looks flat. How a thing looks depends on where you stand.

roots.thread: Take one tin. Lay it down, and it rolls. Stand it up, and it stays. Look at its end and you see a circle, and look at its side and you see a rectangle. It is one tin, and it shows itself in many ways.

teachings.teaching: In this old Buddhist story, a king asks some people who were born blind to feel an elephant. Each one feels a different part. The one who feels the ear says an elephant is like a winnowing basket. The one who feels the foot says it is like a post. Then they quarrel.
teachings.link: One child sees the tin lying down and calls it a roller. Another sees it standing and calls it a stayer. Each of them has met one part of the tin.

teachings.teaching: This Tamil verse says: do not look down on anyone because of how they look. Some people are like the small pin that holds the wheel on a great rolling chariot.
teachings.link: The verse says that the look does not tell you what someone can do. The Slope Test showed the same about things. The tin looked like a roller, and then it stood still.

science.text: A thing with a curved surface and a flat face can roll or stay. It depends on which part touches the ground. Anyone can test this on a slope.

Why is a murre's egg pointed? For many years people said the shape makes it roll in a safe circle. Tests in 2018 found that pointed eggs sit more steadily on a slope. Scientists are still studying which reason matters most.

other_view.view: They say the heaps are ours, but the shape is not. A tin has a curved side and two flat ends whether anyone sorts it or not. It would roll down a hill even if no person had ever seen it.

how_we_found_out.context: How do people find out why a thing has the shape it has? This card tells the true story of a seabird's pointed egg and an idea that turned out to be too simple.
how_we_found_out.story: The common murre is a seabird of cold northern seas. She lays one egg on a bare rock ledge, high on a cliff, with no nest. Her egg is pointed at one end, like a pear. Why? In the 1800s, people said the pointed egg spins like a top in the wind and so stays on the ledge. That was wrong. From the middle of the 1900s, bird books gave another reason. A pointed egg rolls in a curve, as a cone does, so it would roll round and not off the edge. For many years nobody tested this properly. Then Tim Birkhead, a scientist in Britain who had watched murres for more than 40 years, tested real eggs with his team. In 2017 they reported that the egg does roll in a curve, but the curve is often wider than the ledge. In 2018 they put eggs on slopes. The more pointed eggs sat more steadily. So the shape may help the egg to stay still, more than to roll safely.
how_we_found_out.who: Tim Birkhead, Jamie Thompson, Robert Montgomerie and others
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A murre's pointed egg is safe because it spins like a top, or because it rolls in a tight circle. Tests with real eggs showed that it does not spin, and that its rolling circle is often wider than the ledge. On slopes, the pointed eggs were the ones that stayed put best.

Word origins: cylinder from Greek kylindros, 'roller', from kylindein, 'to roll' (Merriam-Webster, Etymonline). Tamil urulai, from urul, 'to roll', used for anything that rolls or is cylindrical, and for a wheel (Wiktionary, citing the Madras Tamil Lexicon). Hindi belan, a rolling pin and also the geometry word for a cylinder (Wiktionary, HinKhoj).
Aryabhata, Aryabhatiya (499 CE): the Earth is round and turns once a day. Taken from the encyclopedia entry on Aryabhata. The exact verse was not looked up.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a family of two in a flat. The Slope Test needs a smooth slope: a steel tray or a laminated board. On a cloth-covered book the matchbox may not slide even at 5 books, so the step tells the parent to lift the end by hand. A grown-up needs about 3 minutes to make the paper cone. On 2 books, a ball, a tin lying across the slope and a cone lying down move, and flat things stay. A cone on a slope swings round its point and often stops, so the table says 'rolled in a curve'. A tall thin tin can topple when it stands on the steep slope, so the list asks for a short one. These slope results come from how such shapes behave and from reasoning. They were not filmed or measured for this lesson, so try the Slope Test once before doing it with your child. Stack It was checked by counting: the tallest tower uses 6 of the 7 things, and the ball is left out. In the cup challenge, two cups taped bottom to bottom roll straight because they rest on two rims of the same size. Two cups taped mouth to mouth rest on the join in the middle, tip to one side and curve again. The game Roll, Slide or Both? was played in the head with 1 and 2 players. A cone is the hardest shape to fetch, so the rules allow a paper one. Step minutes add up to each activity's minutes. Facts looked up on the web while writing: the 2013 dung beetle and Milky Way paper, roller dung beetles in India, the 2017 and 2018 murre egg work, antlion pits, the Indian pangolin curling into a ball, Udana 6.4, Thirukkural 667, the origins of the words cylinder, urulai and belan, and why planets are round. The two museums in the links were looked up, but not their timings. Not fully checked: the exact verse where Aryabhata says the Earth is round. Only an encyclopedia entry was read. The claim that a sliding coin stops sooner than a rolling marble is ordinary physics and was not sourced. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel only, not watched, so watch each one before showing it.
